cues.en: And that's it for this course section.
We repeated the essentials about which you already learned
in the previous course section,
the Remix Essentials course section.
But we also learned about many new features.
We learned about this Layout Route feature
where you have nested routes and folders,
and then file names with the same names as folders
so that you can render the content of one route
nested inside of another route.
You also learned about pathless layout routes
which is the same feature, but without adding a new path.
And you learned how that could, for example,
be used to share some styles across related routes.
You learned about Splat Routes and Resource Routes,
and about all these different kinds of routes in general.
And of course, we also practiced linking
between all these different routes.
You learned about relative links
for this cancel button here.
You learned about programmatic navigation
as we're doing it here.
And you learned about this Search Params feature
which can be used to store some state in the end,
in the URL.
And you learned how that can be used to
build a user interface where one
at the same page can be rendered
and displayed in slightly different ways.
It's the same component,
but some parts of the component are different
based on what's encoded in the URL.
And these are all amazing browser and Remix features,
which you need in almost all kinds of websites
you're going to build.
And therefore, with all these features now out of the way
and covered, we're now ready to dive deeper into Remix.
In this course section,
we're going to continue working
on that expenses demo, application, and website
with which we started in the previous course section.

to the topic of data fetching and mutations.

We're also going to learn how we can use a real database
with our Remix app and with loaders and actions.
And we're then going to dive into slightly more
advanced topics like data submission without forms
or without the form component,
about which you already learned in the essentials section.
We're going to learn how we can share data
between different routes, and we're going to dive
into more important topics that you must know
in order to successfully work with Remix.
Now, as I mentioned in the previous lecture
we are going to continue
with that expenses application.
And attached you'll find the latest snapshot of that project
if you want to continue with that.

This dollar sign JSX file.

because we don't really need that feature
for this demo application.

that we can again work with data,
with loaders and actions,
that we blend some back end logic
with the front end,
as we already did it in the essential section.

to use a real database.

some freight tutorials,

Now what we will use in this course here
is MongoDB's cloud offering

cues.en: So with that, you should have that cluster starting up.

or add an additional IP address,
that should be allowed to talk to the database,
you can do that under database access and network access.

your users and their passwords.

the IP addresses that can talk to the database.

on the MongoDB side to get started
with that database in the Cloud
which we will use in our demo application here.
Now, in that demo application, which we're building,
we wanna use MongoDB.
And in order to talk to it, we'll use a third party library
which will significantly simplify the act
of interacting with that database.
And that library, which we'll use is called Prisma.
Now Prisma is a library that simply makes it very
easy to write code,
which under the hood will be translated to database queries.
So it will make it easier
for us to write code that interacts with a database.
Now, you can learn way more about Prisma
on their official site,
attached you will also find a link
that helps you get started with Prisma.
But you don't need to know anything
about Prisma for this course
because in this course we'll just write some simple,
yet very powerful code that will do everything we wanna do,

So what we wanna do here
is we want to get started with Prisma.

which we see here.
So back in our project, we can run this command to
install this Prisma library into our project.
And then we also copy this command here,
to initialize this project for Prisma usage.

with sequel light, but with MongoDB.

Now what this did is it created a new Prisma folder
and in there a schema.prisma file.

we'll basically set up some things
that will allow us to work with MongoDB.
Now some parts were already set up for us
and we keep that code here.
It, by the way, also created a .n file

for connecting to the database.
And that's indeed the first thing we'll edit.
And for that we go back
to our MongoDB cluster and click on connect,
and then connect your application.
And then there you want to copy this URL
and use that instead of the default URL in that .n file.
And then here you wanna plug in your user's username.
So the MongoDB user, which you created in the last lecture.
In my case it's Max and the password you chose.
And then after this slash here,
before these query parameters,
you can enter the name of the database
in that database cluster,
which we have in this Cloud here,
which will be used for this project.
And here, I'll name it, Remix-expenses.
You can choose any database name here.
Now this connection URL here will be used
by Prisma because of that line of code.
And Prisma will make sure
that it gets access to this .n file.
You don't have to worry about that.
And with that, we got Prisma set up here.
Now we can start creating Prisma models
to tell Prisma how our data should be shaped

and will store it for us in the database under the hood,
and we can thereafter, finally,
write our actions and loaders again.
Now with Prisma installed
it's time to tell Prisma how our data should look like
because Prisma will manage that data for us under the hood
and it will talk to the database under the hood
and store the data there and fetch the data from there.
Now we do tell Prisma how our data looks
like by going to the schema dot prisma file.
And then there you can type model, and then any name
of your choice for that data model you want to define.
And here in my case, I want to have expenses,
so I will give that model a name of expense, not expenses
but expense because even
though we will have multiple expenses
we wanna model one single expense here.
And Prisma will then make sure
that we can also handle multiple expenses.
Thereafter, you add curly braces,
and then you can define your data.
For example, by making sure
that every expense has a unique ID.
That ID in Prisma's world when using MongoDB,
is generally a string.
So it's some text and that has to start with a capital S.
So here we define which field our expense data will have
and which type of data it will be in that field.
And then we have to add some annotations here
for Prisma to store that data correctly
in the MongoDB database.
And here in this schema dot prisma file
we have to add an at ID annotation here.
And by the way, I'm getting some auto completion here
because I installed the Prisma extension for VS code.
You can install that as well
of course to get this auto completion.

Prisma works without that extension as well.

But here we have to add
at ID after this string type annotation, then at default
and there we have to open and close parentheses
and in those parentheses type auto to make sure
that essentially prisma ensures that when data is stored
in MongoDB, a new ID is generated automatically

And then we add at map.
And then in parenthesis, in double quotes underscore id.

ID field in our MongoDB database in which the idea
is stored.

underscore when we work with the data in our code here.

in an underscore ID field.
That's why we store it like this in the database

And then last by the least, we add another annotation
at DB dot object id.

their database.
